mcqs.question: Why does `Grid.isValid()` iterate over a single precomputed `allRegions` list instead of calling separate `checkRows()`, `checkColumns()`, and `checkBoxes()` methods?
options: Because Java cannot compile three separate validation methods in the same class
Because it makes the grid immutable after construction
Because it reduces the total number of cells in the grid from 81 to 27
Because rows, columns, and boxes are all the same shape of constraint — 9 cells that must hold distinct digits — so one Region abstraction and one loop replaces three copies of identical logic
mcqs.explanation: Rows, columns, and boxes are structurally identical constraints (9 cells, all distinct), so representing them as one Region type and looping over all of them avoids duplicating the same duplicate-checking logic three times. There's no such Java restriction, this doesn't affect grid mutability, and the grid still has 81 cells — only the number of Region groupings is 27.

mcqs.question: During backtracking search, why does `canPlace(cell, digit)` check only that cell's three regions instead of re-running full-grid validation?
options: Because a single newly-placed digit can only possibly violate the row, column, and box it belongs to — checking the other 24 regions again is redundant work repeated on every candidate placement
Because full-grid validation would give incorrect results after the first move
Because Region objects are deleted after each check and must be avoided
Because it lowers the maximum grid size the solver can support
mcqs.explanation: A single cell change can only affect the three regions that cell is a member of — every other region is untouched by that move, so re-checking them is wasted work, especially at the scale of thousands of placements during backtracking. Full-grid validation still gives correct results, Regions aren't deleted between checks, and grid size is unrelated.

mcqs.question: When asked in an interview to design a Sudoku solver from scratch, which approach should you lead with, and why?
options: Constraint propagation with full candidate tracking, since it's always strictly faster than backtracking
Plain backtracking, since it's correct, explainable in the available time, and a solid baseline you can then optimize if asked
A brute-force check of every possible 9^81 grid combination, filtering for validity
Machine learning trained on solved puzzles, since it generalizes to any puzzle difficulty
mcqs.explanation: Backtracking is the right first answer because it's correct, reasonably simple to implement live, and gives you a working baseline to optimize from if the interviewer pushes for more speed. Constraint propagation is a valid follow-up optimization, not a required starting point, and can add overhead on easy puzzles; iterating over 9^81 grids is computationally absurd; and ML solving isn't the expected approach for a design-and-implement interview.
